title: OT Risk Appetite & Exposure Assessment
framing: This high-level assessment is led by interview. It sets an organisation's inherent risk exposure, meaning what it faces because of its sector, criticality, geopolitical position and threat context, against its apparent risk appetite, meaning how much cyber risk it appears willing to accept, and judges how well the two fit. The fit is the finding. An organisation that accepts materially more risk than its exposure warrants has usually drifted there without deciding to. The assessor leads throughout, starting from sector baselines and working through a structured interview. An optional technical review checks the stated appetite against the state of the systems. The assessment draws on NIST SP 800-82, the NIST CSF, the risk approach of IEC 62443-3-2 and the terms of ISO 31000, but it is not an assessment against any one standard.
sourceNote: The structure and band definitions draw on the risk governance concepts in NIST SP 800-82 and the NIST CSF, the consequence-driven risk approach of IEC 62443-3-2, the risk appetite terms of ISO 31000, and practitioner judgement. The sector baselines and band definitions are SolutionsPT starting points and do not decide any result.
criticalCaveats: This is a characterisation based on expert judgement. It does not measure the organisation against a standard. Neither exposure nor appetite is scored objectively, and both are the assessor's professional judgement.
No risk appetite band is good or bad in itself, and the finding is the fit between exposure and appetite. A cautious appetite is better than a tolerant one only when it suits the exposure better.
The report gives the client's leadership a basis for deciding consciously which risks to accept. It does not determine whether their appetite is correct.

setup.question: Organisation sector (sets the exposure baseline)
setup.drives: Sets the starting exposure band for the EXP items, which the assessor confirms or changes.

setup.question: Include the optional technical review (revealed appetite)?
setup.drives: Adds the TECH section, so stated and revealed appetite can be compared.

sections.name: Inherent risk exposure
sections.summary: This section rates what the organisation faces because of what it is and where it operates. Start from the sector baseline, then adjust for threat, geopolitics, consequence, regulation and connections to others to reach an exposure band from limited to severe.

sections.name: Apparent risk appetite
sections.summary: This section rates how much cyber risk the organisation appears willing to accept. The interview covers governance, investment, remediation, risk acceptance, operational trade-offs, safety and past incidents, and gives an appetite band from averse to tolerant.

sections.name: Revealed appetite (technical, optional)
sections.summary: This section checks the stated appetite against the state of patching, segmentation, monitoring, access and recovery. A gap between what was said in interview and what the systems show is a finding in its own right.

items.title: Sector and criticality
items.stateSummary: How critical is the organisation's function? Its sector and criticality set the baseline exposure.
items.interviewPrompt: Set the sector baseline, then adjust it for how essential or critical this organisation's function is.
items.rationale: Sector and criticality set the floor for every other reading. A safety-critical essential service is in a very different position from a discrete manufacturer, whatever either chooses to do. This is the largest single factor in inherent exposure, so it is the place to start.
items.assessorRecords: characterisation (free text) + contribution to the section's band

bandAnchors.limited: The organisation has no essential-service or safety role. An outage inconveniences customers but harms nobody.
bandAnchors.moderate: The organisation matters to its customers or a supply chain, but alternatives exist, and an outage is costly but not dangerous.
bandAnchors.high: The organisation runs an essential or regulated service, or a site whose processes are safety-relevant. An outage affects many people or other organisations' operations.
bandAnchors.severe: The organisation is critical national infrastructure or a designated essential service, where loss of function has public-safety or national consequences.

items.title: Threat and targeting context
items.stateSummary: Who plausibly targets this organisation, and are they commodity attackers, criminal groups or state-level actors?
items.interviewPrompt: Who are the credible threat actors? Is there evidence of targeted interest in this sector or organisation? Is the threat limited to commodity ransomware, or does it include advanced or state-level actors?
items.rationale: Exposure depends on who is trying to attack the organisation as well as on what could go wrong in theory. An organisation facing only commodity ransomware is in a different position from one credibly targeted by capable or state-level actors. Treating the two as the same misjudges the size of the risk.
items.assessorRecords: characterisation (free text) + contribution to the section's band

bandAnchors.limited: Only untargeted, opportunistic threats are credible, with no sign of interest in the organisation or its sector.
bandAnchors.moderate: Exposed to commodity ransomware and fraud like most organisations, with no evidence of targeting beyond that.
bandAnchors.high: The sector has seen targeted campaigns by capable criminal groups, and the organisation is a plausible target for them.
bandAnchors.severe: State-aligned or similarly capable actors have shown credible interest in the sector or the organisation itself, including intrusions into operational systems.

items.title: Geopolitical exposure
items.stateSummary: Do the organisation's location, ownership, markets or sector put it in a geopolitically exposed position?
items.interviewPrompt: Consider where the organisation operates, whether its sector is contested, its ownership and supply ties, and any current geopolitical tension that affects it. Record your judgement and the reasons for it.
items.rationale: Geopolitical position changes exposure in ways the sector alone does not capture. Ownership ties, region of operation and tension around the sector can all raise targeting sharply. This reading depends on the assessor's own judgement more than any other, so the prompt raises the question and leaves the answer to the assessor.
items.assessorRecords: characterisation (free text) + contribution to the section's band

bandAnchors.limited: Operations are domestic only, in a sector that draws no geopolitical attention.
bandAnchors.moderate: There is some international supply chain or ownership, but no contested region or politically sensitive service.
bandAnchors.high: The sector is named in national threat reporting, or the organisation operates in or supplies a region under geopolitical pressure.
bandAnchors.severe: Operations, ownership or customers sit in a contested region, or the service is one a hostile state would plausibly want to disrupt.

items.title: Consequence of compromise
items.stateSummary: How severe would the real-world consequence of a serious compromise be, whether operational, financial, safety, environmental or systemic?
items.interviewPrompt: What is the worst credible consequence? Could it threaten life or the environment? Is it systemic, because others depend on the organisation? Or is it purely operational and financial?
items.rationale: Exposure comes down to consequence, and in OT the worst credible consequence can be physical, such as injury, an environmental release or the loss of an essential service. An honest view of consequence separates a serious exposure from one that is merely inconvenient.
items.assessorRecords: characterisation (free text) + contribution to the section's band

bandAnchors.limited: The worst credible outcome is contained: lost data or downtime, with no safety, environmental or public impact.
bandAnchors.moderate: The worst credible outcome is significant financial loss or production downtime, with no harm to people or the environment.
bandAnchors.high: The worst credible outcome is serious operational disruption, a reportable environmental release, or harm to people that existing safeguards would probably limit.
bandAnchors.severe: The worst credible outcome is loss of life, a major environmental incident, or the loss of an essential service to a large population.

items.title: Regulatory and obligation weight
items.stateSummary: How much regulatory exposure does the organisation carry, for example under NIS2 or the CAF, sector regulation, or the CRA as a supplier?
items.interviewPrompt: Which regulatory regimes apply, and how heavy are the obligations they bring?
items.rationale: Regulatory weight indicates the scrutiny an organisation faces and the posture it is expected to hold, and non-compliance is an exposure in its own right. Regulation also shapes what outsiders will see as an acceptable appetite.
items.assessorRecords: characterisation (free text) + contribution to the section's band

bandAnchors.limited: No sector-specific cyber regulation applies, only general obligations such as data protection.
bandAnchors.moderate: Some sector requirements or contractual obligations from customers apply, but they are lightly enforced.
bandAnchors.high: In scope of NIS, NIS2, the CAF or an equivalent regime, with a regulator who inspects and can impose penalties.
bandAnchors.severe: Heavy, specific regulation applies, with licence or safety-case consequences, as in nuclear or major hazard regimes, so a cyber failure can halt operations.

items.title: Interconnection and supply-chain reach
items.stateSummary: How large and exposed are the organisation's attack surface and its web of dependencies?
items.interviewPrompt: Consider how the organisation connects to others, what access third parties and vendors have, and how far the supply chain reaches in both directions.
items.rationale: A large, interconnected attack surface with deep third-party access raises exposure whatever the sector, because it multiplies the ways in. Supply-chain reach matters in both directions, covering what can reach the organisation and what it can reach.
items.assessorRecords: characterisation (free text) + contribution to the section's band

bandAnchors.limited: The organisation is largely self-contained, with few external connections, and no other organisation depends on its systems.
bandAnchors.moderate: The organisation has ordinary business connections to suppliers and customers, with some remote access for support.
bandAnchors.high: There are many remote sites or integrators with standing access, or other organisations rely on its services to operate.
bandAnchors.severe: The organisation is a hub that others depend on, or has a large estate of third-party and remote connections into operational systems, so a compromise spreads well beyond it.

items.title: Board and governance attention
items.stateSummary: How seriously, and how actively, does senior governance treat cyber risk to operations?
items.interviewPrompt: How does the board engage with OT cyber risk? Is it a standing agenda item, or does it come up only after incidents? Who owns it? Listen for whether it is governed as a business risk or delegated as an IT matter.
items.rationale: The way senior governance treats cyber risk is the strongest single signal of the real appetite, because it decides whether everything below it is resourced and owned. Risk that never reaches the board is accepted by default, whatever the policy says.
items.assessorRecords: characterisation (free text) + contribution to the section's band

bandAnchors.averse: Cyber risk is a standing board item with a named owner, regular reporting on the risk being carried, and real challenge from the board.
bandAnchors.cautious: Cyber is on the board agenda and owned by an executive, though reporting covers status more than the risk being carried.
bandAnchors.open: Cyber reaches the board occasionally, usually after an incident or an audit, and ownership sits below board level.
bandAnchors.tolerant: The board rarely discusses cyber and no executive owns it. It is treated as an IT matter.

items.title: Investment stance
items.stateSummary: How well does the organisation resource cyber security for the exposure it faces?
items.interviewPrompt: Is security funded in advance, or only in reaction to events? Is the spend treated as investment or as cost? How does it fare against competing priorities?
items.rationale: What an organisation funds shows its priorities more reliably than what it says. Spending that only ever reacts to events points to a higher tolerance of risk than most such organisations would admit.
items.assessorRecords: characterisation (free text) + contribution to the section's band

bandAnchors.averse: Security is funded ahead of need, operational technology included, and the funding is protected when budgets tighten.
bandAnchors.cautious: A dedicated budget covers the main risks, though some operational technology work waits for capital cycles.
bandAnchors.open: Security competes with other spending and is funded when a specific case is made. Operational technology work is often deferred.
bandAnchors.tolerant: There is little or no dedicated funding. Security spending is reactive and mostly follows incidents or audit findings.

items.title: Remediation urgency
items.stateSummary: How quickly does the organisation act on known risks and findings?
items.interviewPrompt: When a serious finding or vulnerability is identified, what happens next, and how fast? Listen for any gap between policy and practice.
items.rationale: Stated and real appetite most often part company over how fast known risks are dealt with. An organisation that finds problems but fixes them slowly is accepting the risk in practice, however cautious it says it is.
items.assessorRecords: characterisation (free text) + contribution to the section's band

bandAnchors.averse: Findings are fixed to defined timescales, in operational systems as well as IT, and overdue items are escalated.
bandAnchors.cautious: Findings have owners and target dates. Dates in operational systems slip for outage windows but are tracked.
bandAnchors.open: Findings are logged but dates move freely, and a backlog of old findings is accepted as normal.
bandAnchors.tolerant: Findings are rarely tracked to closure, and the same issues come back from one assessment to the next.

items.title: Conscious risk acceptance
items.stateSummary: Does the organisation accept risk deliberately and on the record, or does risk build up by default?
items.interviewPrompt: What risk does the organisation knowingly accept? Is each acceptance documented and owned, or has risk built up without anyone deciding? The answer separates a considered appetite from an accidental one.
items.rationale: Appetite turns on whether risk is accepted deliberately or by drift. An organisation with a considered appetite documents and owns the risk it tolerates. One with an accidental appetite builds up unmanaged risk that nobody chose, and this is the finding the assessment most often makes.
items.assessorRecords: characterisation (free text) + contribution to the section's band

bandAnchors.averse: Every accepted risk is documented, owned, signed off at the right level and given an expiry date.
bandAnchors.cautious: Significant risks are formally accepted with an owner, though expiry and review are not always enforced.
bandAnchors.open: Risk acceptance is informal. Decisions happen in meetings or by moving a date, with little on record.
bandAnchors.tolerant: There is no acceptance process. Risk is carried by default, and nobody could say what has been accepted.

items.title: Tolerance for operational disruption vs security
items.stateSummary: How does the organisation weigh security work against operational continuity?
items.interviewPrompt: When security work such as patching, segmentation or planned downtime conflicts with production, which wins, and who decides?
items.rationale: When security work clashes with production, the choice made, and who makes it, shows the organisation's priorities under pressure. Anyone can state an appetite, but the trade-off decision shows the real one.
items.assessorRecords: characterisation (free text) + contribution to the section's band

bandAnchors.averse: Security work takes priority, and the organisation will schedule downtime or accept cost to reduce risk.
bandAnchors.cautious: Security work is planned into maintenance windows and rarely refused, though availability comes first.
bandAnchors.open: Security work is often postponed because operations will not release the plant, and no alternative is arranged.
bandAnchors.tolerant: Security changes are routinely refused on operational grounds, and nobody weighs the risk of not making them.

items.title: Safety framing
items.stateSummary: Is cyber risk to OT understood as a safety issue, or purely as a business or IT one?
items.interviewPrompt: Does the organisation connect OT cyber risk to physical safety, or treat it as a data or IT risk? In high-consequence sectors the answer says a lot about the real appetite.
items.rationale: Whether an organisation sees OT cyber risk as a safety matter or an IT one is a strong predictor of how seriously it treats it, especially in high-consequence sectors. Treating a safety-relevant system as a data risk is itself a sign that appetite has been misjudged.
items.assessorRecords: characterisation (free text) + contribution to the section's band

bandAnchors.averse: Cyber is treated as a safety hazard: it appears in the safety case, in hazard studies and in safety sign-off.
bandAnchors.cautious: Cyber is recognised as a contributor to safety risk and named in safety documentation, though not fully analysed.
bandAnchors.open: Cyber and safety are managed separately. The link is acknowledged but not acted on.
bandAnchors.tolerant: Cyber is not seen as relevant to safety, and safety engineers play no part in it.

items.title: Response to past incidents / near-misses
items.stateSummary: What does the organisation's history show about its real appetite?
items.interviewPrompt: How has the organisation responded to past incidents or near misses? Did they lead to lasting change, or did things go back to normal?
items.rationale: How an organisation behaves after a real incident or near miss shows its appetite more honestly than any interview answer, because it shows what the organisation does under pressure. Lasting change means the appetite shifted. A return to normal means it never moved.
items.assessorRecords: characterisation (free text) + contribution to the section's band

bandAnchors.averse: Incidents and near misses, including those elsewhere in the sector, lead to reviews and funded changes that are seen through.
bandAnchors.cautious: The organisation's own incidents lead to real changes, though near misses and incidents elsewhere get less attention.
bandAnchors.open: Incidents are fixed locally, but the lessons are not carried across the organisation.
bandAnchors.tolerant: Incidents are treated as bad luck. Little changes afterwards, and near misses go unrecorded.

items.title: Patching and update reality
items.stateSummary: How far behind is patching, and how disciplined are updates? The answer shows the appetite in practice.
items.interviewPrompt: How often are OT systems patched and updated in practice, and how long do fixes wait before they are applied?
items.rationale: Patching lag is one of the most direct measures of tolerated risk. The time between a fix becoming available and being applied is risk accepted, whether knowingly or not. It is a good check on a stated cautious appetite.
items.assessorRecords: characterisation (free text) + contribution to the section's band

bandAnchors.averse: Operational systems are updated on a defined cycle, with vendor-approved updates tested and applied.
bandAnchors.cautious: Updates are applied during planned outages. Exceptions exist, but they are recorded and the risk is compensated.
bandAnchors.open: Updates happen irregularly, usually when a vendor visits. Many systems are well behind, and exceptions are not tracked.
bandAnchors.tolerant: There is no update regime for operational systems. Unsupported operating systems and years-old firmware are left in place.

items.title: Segmentation and architecture state
items.stateSummary: Does the network as built match the stated security posture?
items.interviewPrompt: Is the OT network segmented in practice, or flat behind a perimeter?
items.rationale: Network architecture shows how much lateral-movement risk is accepted, whatever the organisation says about segmentation. A flat network behind a perimeter, in an organisation that claims to be cautious, is a clear gap between stated and revealed appetite.
items.assessorRecords: characterisation (free text) + contribution to the section's band

bandAnchors.averse: Operational networks are divided into zones with controlled connections between them, and the boundary with IT is enforced and reviewed.
bandAnchors.cautious: A clear boundary with IT exists and critical systems are separated, though zoning inside the operational network is partial.
bandAnchors.open: A single boundary separates IT from the operational network, with little separation behind it.
bandAnchors.tolerant: IT and operational networks are effectively flat, or the boundary carries broad exceptions that nobody reviews.

items.title: Monitoring and detection coverage
items.stateSummary: Could the organisation detect a compromise of the systems it says it cares about?
items.interviewPrompt: What monitoring and detection covers the OT systems in practice?
items.rationale: Detection coverage tests whether the organisation would even know if a risk it claims to care about came about. Low coverage alongside a cautious stated appetite means the caution exists on paper only.
items.assessorRecords: characterisation (free text) + contribution to the section's band

bandAnchors.averse: Operational networks are monitored for unusual activity, and alerts reach people who can act on them at any hour.
bandAnchors.cautious: The main boundaries and critical systems are monitored, though coverage inside operational networks is partial.
bandAnchors.open: Monitoring covers the IT estate, but operational systems are largely unseen.
bandAnchors.tolerant: Nothing is in place that would reveal an intrusion into operational systems.

items.title: Access and remote-access control
items.stateSummary: This item looks at privileged and remote access into OT as it works in practice.
items.interviewPrompt: How are remote, vendor and privileged access to OT controlled in practice?
items.rationale: Privileged and remote access into OT is a direct measure of tolerated exposure, because standing open access is among the highest-impact risks. Where policy claims control but practice allows standing access, the practice is the revealed appetite.
items.assessorRecords: characterisation (free text) + contribution to the section's band

bandAnchors.averse: Individual accounts and strong authentication are used throughout, and remote access is approved for each session and recorded.
bandAnchors.cautious: Accounts are named and remote access uses multi-factor authentication, with a few shared or standing accounts kept under control.
bandAnchors.open: Shared accounts are common, and some suppliers have standing remote access.
bandAnchors.tolerant: Default or long-unchanged shared passwords are in use, and remote access is always on and unrecorded.

items.title: Backup and recovery reality
items.stateSummary: Does the ability to recover match the resilience the organisation claims?
items.interviewPrompt: Do OT backups exist, including controller logic and configuration? Are they protected, and has a restore been tested?
items.rationale: Recovery is where claims of resilience get tested. Untested or unprotected backups mean the organisation is accepting far more consequence risk than its stated posture implies. The gap between the recovery it claims and the recovery it can demonstrate is revealed appetite.
items.assessorRecords: characterisation (free text) + contribution to the section's band

bandAnchors.averse: Configurations and critical data are backed up offline, and restores are tested against an agreed recovery time.
bandAnchors.cautious: Regular backups exist and a restore has been tested at least once, though not for every system.
bandAnchors.open: Backups are taken, but no restore has ever been tested and no recovery time is agreed.
bandAnchors.tolerant: Backups are ad hoc or missing, or kept where a compromise would also reach them, and nobody has tried a restore.

output.narrative: Prose characterising (1) the organisation's inherent exposure and why, (2) its apparent appetite and what reveals it, (3) the coherence between them (aligned, under-protected, or over-invested) as the headline, and (4) where the technical layer is used, any stated-vs-revealed gap. Written as a board-facing basis for a conscious risk-acceptance conversation.

visual.spec: Two-axis plot: inherent exposure (limited->severe) on one axis, apparent appetite (averse->tolerant) on the other. Organisation placed as a point. Diagonal = coherence. Point below the coherence line (appetite more tolerant than exposure warrants) = under-protected, marked as the main finding; above = over-invested. This single chart is the report headline.
visual.secondary: Optional stated-vs-revealed marker: plot both the interview-derived and technical-derived appetite positions to show the gap.

_contentNote: 6 exposure + 7 appetite + 5 optional technical items, each with an interview prompt and a rationale. Coherence scoring (risk-appetite-coherence), narrative + exposure-vs-appetite visual. Assessor-led with sector baselines and prompts. Draft bands/baselines are a tunable house scaffold for the consultant to evaluate and adjust.
_relatedWork: Sibling to the OT posture/health-check screener in look, feel and high-level assessor-led character - but a different scoring model (coherence, not a better-is-higher grade). Sits in the screeners family.
